title: The Acquisition Illusion

More users, more market share, more downloads. Another move in the race for technical supremacy. I see something else happening. Press enter or click to view image in full size Photo by jhenning via Pixabay under Pixabay Content License Cropped from original Google isn’t primarily trying to acquire users but move the ones it already has. While the tech industry remains fixated on algorithmic benchmarks, Google is preparing to pull off an heist on the everyday habits of ordinary users. They already own many of the places where people spend their digital lives. Chrome, Android, Search, Gmail, YouTube, Workspace. The doors are open. Millions of people walk through them every day. What happens once they’re inside ? You Can Lead a Horse to Water In product, acquisition and activation solve different problems. Acquisition brings people in and activation gets them to experience a product’s value, when that experience becomes useful enough, frequent enough, and familiar enough then a new behavior can become a habit. Google has a distribution advantage that most competitors can only dream of. It doesn’t need to introduce an entirely new destination into people’s lives, It can put Gemini in front of users who already open Google products dozens of times a day. In theory, the transition should be straightforward. Add a button, change a user journey and make the assistant more visible, but the conversational assistance isn’t just another feature to discover. For decades, Google has trained us to perform a very specific ritual : type a few keywords, scan a list of links, click, compare, repeat. This gestures are almost automatic, we don’t have to think about how to search. We just do it. the conversational assistance proposes a different ritual: articulate an intention, describe a problem, accept a synthesis, delegate part of the work. The shift sounds simple, It isn’t! Google isn’t introducing another interface, It’s asking people to change a reflex they’ve spent years learning. And a reflex doesn’t change just because a button appears in an app. Newton’s First Law Google’s problem isn’t visibility. It’s behavioral inertia. A user opens Search because they need to find something. They open Gmail because they need to reply to a message. They open Calendar when they’re looking for a time slot and in those moments, they’re focused on a specific task, they’re not exploring, they’re not try to learn a new way of interacting with their tools. In-app messaging runs into a familiar limitation: the more focused people are, the more aggressively they ignore anything that doesn’t help them complete the task at hand. Prompts, suggestions, banners, all become noise. External advertising plays a different role. It reaches people before the moment of use, when they’re not busy searching, answering emails, or scheduling appointments. Its job isn’t to convert them on the spot but plant an idea: Next time I need to prepare for a job interview, I could just ask Gemini. And That’s audience activation not acquisition. The Industry Is Looking Elsewhere Here’s where things get strategically interesting. For industry insiders, attention is locked on the race for algorithmic performance. Who has the best model ? The highest benchmark scores ? The largest context window ? Challengers like Anthropic, OpenAI, and Perplexity keep feeding the narrative of technical supremacy. Most people don’t choose their everyday tools by comparing benchmark scores. They want to prepare for an interview, plan a trip, organize their lives, help a child with a project, or get through an administrative task without losing an afternoon. They have heard of Claude at the coffee machine, evaluation arenas, or model parameters is non sense for them. That doesn’t mean they’re indifferent to technology. It means technical performance is rarely the language in which they evaluate an everyday product. Google understands the disconnect. The ads don’t ask people to appreciate the technology. They show them something they might want to get done, the distinction matters. A technically impressive product still has to find its way into ordinary life, the user has to recognize a problem, imagine a solution, try it, and decide whether the experience is worth repeating. Google’s advantage lies in its ability to introduce this possibility to people who already use its products day to day. The question is no longer simply who designs the most efficient system, but which one becomes people’s first choice when they need help, or which one is simply the most accessible. Back to the Future Watching this strategy unfold, I can’t help thinking of Microsoft and Netscape. In the 90’s, Microsoft dominated the operating system market. Then the web emerged as a different kind of threat. If the browser became the primary gateway to computing, Windows risked losing its central position. Microsoft’s response was to bundle Internet Explorer directly into its operating system, using its installed base to defend its position. The comparison with Google isn’t exact.
